topics.name: Plato
topics.kicker: Greek philosopher · Student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle
topics.briefing: Plato was a Greek philosopher who admired his teacher Socrates so much that he spent his life writing conversations starring him, even after Athens executed Socrates for his ideas. Plato’s dialogues introduced some of philosophy’s most famous images, like the Allegory of the Cave, which compares most people to prisoners who mistake shadows for reality. He also founded a school called the Academy, where he trained his own star student, Aristotle.

tossups.p: In one of this man’s dialogues, a character asks whether something is holy because the gods love it, or whether the gods love it because it is already holy, a puzzle called the Euthyphro [“yoo-THIF-roh”] dilemma. This man founded the Academy in Athens; a later school there that carried on his teachings was closed by a Byzantine emperor in 529 CE.
tossups.r: This man wrote almost all his philosophy as dialogues starring his own teacher. For 10 points, name this Greek thinker, a student of Socrates who wrote the _Republic_, describing an ideal city ruled by philosopher-kings.

tossups.p: None of this man’s teacher’s own spoken words survive directly, since that teacher never wrote anything down, leaving this man as the main source for his ideas. This man also argued that the soul is immortal and already knows eternal truths before birth, merely needing to recall them.
tossups.r: In one dialogue, that same teacher calmly refuses a friend’s offer to help him escape from prison rather than break an unwritten agreement with his city. For 10 points, name this philosopher whose Allegory of the Cave compares ordinary people to prisoners mistaking shadows for reality.

tossups.p: In a pair of this man’s dialogues, a character named Timaeus explains the origin of the universe while another named Critias tells the earliest surviving story of a lost island called Atlantis. In a third dialogue, guests at a banquet take turns praising the nature of love.
tossups.r: This man argued that ordinary objects are just flawed copies of perfect, unchanging ideas he called Forms. For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher who taught Aristotle and wrote the _Republic_.

tossups.p: This man suggested that artists and poets should be banned from his ideal city because their work is merely an imitation of an imitation of the truth. At a banquet in one of this man’s dialogues, the comic playwright Aristophanes [“air-is-TOFF-uh-neez”] jokes that humans were once double-bodied beings split apart, forever searching for their other half.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher whose dialogue the _Symposium_ explores the nature of love.

tossups.p: This man described an ideal city-state called Kallipolis, ruled by specially trained guardians, in his most famous work. In that same dialogue, a character named Glaucon tells the story of a magic ring that could make its wearer invisible, asking whether people act justly only out of fear of getting caught.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher who wrote the _Republic_ and studied under Socrates.

tossups.p: This man was reportedly so shaken when an Athenian jury condemned his teacher to death that he turned away from a career in politics and toward philosophy instead. He later wrote down that teacher’s trial defense, including the claim that the teacher’s wisdom came only from knowing that he knew nothing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this author of the _Apology_, a student of Socrates who also wrote the _Republic_.

tossups.p: This man wrote that most people are like prisoners chained inside a cave, mistaking shadows on a wall for the whole of reality. He compared escaping that cave and seeing the sun outside to the long, difficult climb toward true knowledge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher whose Allegory of the Cave appears in his dialogue the _Republic_.

tossups.p: This man’s dialogues are mostly named after the other characters who speak in them rather than after himself. In the _Crito_, one of those characters refuses a wealthy friend’s offer to bribe guards and flee an Athenian prison.
tossups.r: That character, Socrates, appears throughout this man’s writing. For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher who taught Aristotle at his school, the Academy.

tossups.p: At a dinner party in one of this man’s dialogues, a drunken Alcibiades [“al-sih-BY-uh-deez”] arrives late and praises his teacher’s legendary self-control. This man’s dialogues are set almost entirely in Athens and nearby cities during his own teacher’s lifetime.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher whose _Symposium_ and _Republic_ both feature his teacher, Socrates, as the main speaker.

tossups.p: This man taught that learning is really just remembering truths the soul already knew before it was born into a body. He used the image of a divided line to rank different kinds of knowledge, from shadowy guesses up to pure understanding of his highest Forms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher, the teacher of Aristotle and student of Socrates.

tossups.p: This man’s uncle Charmides and his mother’s relative Critias both took part in a brief, violent government that ruled Athens before this man turned to philosophy instead of politics. This man traveled to Sicily more than once, hoping unsuccessfully to turn a tyrant of Syracuse into a philosopher-king.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Athenian thinker who wrote the _Republic_ and founded the Academy.

tossups.p: This man compared the human soul to a chariot pulled by two horses, one noble and one unruly, guided by a charioteer representing reason. In another dialogue, he argued that true love should rise from admiring one beautiful body to finally admiring Beauty itself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher whose dialogues the _Phaedrus_ and _Symposium_ explore love, and who studied under Socrates.

tossups.p: This man founded a school on the outskirts of Athens named for the hero Academus, where students reportedly studied geometry before being admitted. A sign over its door is said to have warned that no one ignorant of geometry should enter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher who founded the Academy and taught Aristotle there.

tossups.p: This man’s dialogue the _Phaedo_ depicts his teacher calmly discussing the immortality of the soul on the very day that teacher is executed by drinking poison. This man was not present himself at that final scene, by his own account in the text.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher who wrote of Socrates’s death and later wrote the _Republic_.

tossups.p: This man used the sun as a symbol for his highest Form, the Form of the Good, which he said makes all other knowledge possible to see clearly. He explained this idea shortly before his more famous story of prisoners watching shadows on a cave wall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher whose Allegory of the Cave and theory of Forms appear in the _Republic_.

trap.title: Teacher, student, or Plato himself?
trap.body: Three names travel together in almost every clue: Socrates (his teacher and the main character of his dialogues), Plato himself (the author), and Aristotle (his student). A clue describing what a character says or does inside a dialogue — like refusing to escape prison, or claiming to know nothing — is usually describing Socrates the character, not Plato the author who wrote it down.
trap.fix: Ask who is being credited with writing versus who is simply talking in the scene. “Wrote,” “author of,” or a named dialogue title (_Republic_, _Symposium_, _Apology_) points to Plato. A direct quotation or action “inside” a dialogue usually belongs to Socrates.

topics.name: René Descartes
topics.kicker: French philosopher and mathematician · Father of mind-body dualism
topics.briefing: René Descartes wanted to doubt absolutely everything until he found one fact he could not deny: that he was thinking, and therefore he existed. That idea, “I think, therefore I am,” first appeared in his _Discourse on the Method_, and his most famous book, _Meditations on First Philosophy_, argued that mind and body are two separate kinds of things. He was a brilliant mathematician too: the x-y graph used in math class is called the “Cartesian plane” in his honor.

sample.note: 15 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (4 Middle School/Easy High School + 11 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This thinker opened a six-part work with a chapter called “What Can Be Called Into Doubt,” arguing that since dreams can feel just as real as waking life, the senses alone prove nothing for certain. To push that doubt even further, he imagined an evil demon bent on deceiving him about absolutely everything.
tossups.r: He decided that the one thing he could not doubt was his own thinking. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who wrote _Meditations on First Philosophy_ and concluded, “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed this thinker to explain how an immaterial mind could possibly move a physical body, a puzzle later called the “problem of interaction.” This thinker believed that the two met inside a small structure in the brain called the pineal gland.
tossups.r: He had described mind and body as two completely separate kinds of substance in his _Meditations on First Philosophy_. For 10 points, name this French rationalist who wrote “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: This thinker used a piece of wax that keeps changing shape, smell, and texture as it melts to argue that only reason, not the senses, can ever truly understand what an object is. He split all of reality into thinking substance and extended, physical substance.
tossups.r: That split is now called mind-body dualism. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who proposed this theory in _Meditations on First Philosophy_ and declared, “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: This thinker imagined a thousand-sided shape called a chiliagon [“KIL-ee-uh-gon”] to show that the mind can understand an idea clearly through reason even when it cannot picture it through imagination. He also distinguished ideas that are innate, invented, or received from the senses.
tossups.r: This thinker argued that because he had an idea of a perfect, infinite being, that being, God, must exist. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who wrote _Meditations on First Philosophy_.

tossups.p: As a mathematician, this thinker devised a rule for counting how many positive and negative roots a polynomial equation can have, now called his Rule of Signs. He also pioneered analytic geometry, the use of algebra to study geometric shapes.
tossups.r: The x-y coordinate grid used in graphing is named for him. For 10 points, name this French thinker and mathematician who also wrote “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: Twentieth-century philosopher Gilbert Ryle mocked one of this man’s ideas as the “ghost in the machine” and called it a “category mistake” in his book _The Concept of Mind_. Ryle was attacking this man’s theory that the mind and body are two separate substances.
tossups.r: That theory is now called mind-body dualism. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who proposed it in _Meditations on First Philosophy_.

tossups.p: Critics including Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Gassendi wrote formal objections to this thinker’s most famous book, and he published his point-by-point answers alongside them as “Objections and Replies.” Some critics accused him of circular reasoning in his proof that God exists.
tossups.r: That accusation is sometimes called his namesake “circle.” For 10 points, name this French philosopher whose _Meditations on First Philosophy_ drew all those objections.

tossups.p: After years of living quietly in the Dutch Republic, this thinker traveled to Sweden at the invitation of Queen Christina, who wanted him to tutor her in philosophy. He caught pneumonia there in the harsh winter and died in 1650.
tossups.r: Years earlier, he had written that the one thing he could never doubt was his own thinking. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who declared, “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: In his final book, this thinker explained emotions like wonder, love, and hatred as being caused by the movement of tiny “animal spirits” through the nerves. That book, written near the end of his life, was called _The Passions of the Soul_.
tossups.r: Earlier, in _Meditations on First Philosophy_, this same thinker had argued that mind and body are entirely separate things. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who wrote “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: This thinker’s most famous book opens with a section explaining what can be “called into doubt,” before moving on to an argument built around a melting piece of wax, which he said only the intellect, and not the senses, can truly know.
tossups.r: That book also describes an all-powerful evil demon devoted to deception. For 10 points, name this French philosopher whose _Meditations on First Philosophy_ concludes that mind and body are separate substances.

tossups.p: This thinker’s work often just called his _Discourse_ laid out a four-step method for reasoning clearly and first stated the idea known in Latin as “cogito, ergo sum.” He also used that method of radical doubt to question even basic mathematics.
tossups.r: That phrase translates to “I think, therefore I am.” For 10 points, name this French philosopher and mathematician, the namesake of the Cartesian coordinate plane.

tossups.p: This thinker compared the usual view of how a mind controls a body to a sailor simply steering a ship, before arguing that the true relationship feels much closer and more “intermingled” than that. He is also remembered for describing a deceptive evil demon.
tossups.r: That demon appears in his _Meditations on First Philosophy_, which also proposes mind-body dualism. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who wrote “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: Besides his philosophy, this man worked out a law describing how light bends when it passes from one medium into another, publishing it as an essay on optics alongside his famous _Discourse_. That law of refraction is sometimes named jointly for him and Snell.
tossups.r: In philosophy, this same man is remembered for radical doubt and for saying “I think, therefore I am.” For 10 points, name this French thinker, the namesake of the Cartesian coordinate system.

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that children are born with certain innate ideas already present in the mind, a claim that English thinkers who believed in the “blank slate” would later reject. He also believed that knowledge built on reason was more reliable than knowledge built on the senses.
tossups.r: That approach makes him one of the first great rationalists. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who wrote _Meditations on First Philosophy_ and declared, “I think, therefore I am.”

tossups.p: This thinker spent much of his adult life living quietly in the Dutch Republic, away from France, so he could write and study in peace. While there, he corresponded with Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia about how the mind and body interact.
tossups.r: He is considered the father of modern philosophy and of analytic geometry. For 10 points, name this French thinker who wrote _Meditations on First Philosophy_ and concluded, “I think, therefore I am.”

trap.title: Rationalist, not empiricist
trap.body: Real tossups often pile on words like “philosopher,” “doubt,” and “innate ideas” that also fit other Enlightenment thinkers. Mixing this man up with a British empiricist like John Locke, who argued the mind starts as a blank slate with no innate ideas, is the single most common wrong buzz, since the two philosophers argue almost the exact opposite point.
trap.fix: This man’s clues are rationalist: innate ideas, doubting the senses, an evil demon, melting wax, mind-body dualism, and the Cartesian coordinate plane. Locke’s clues are empiricist: tabula rasa, no innate ideas, knowledge from experience, and natural rights to life, liberty, and property.

topics.name: John Locke
topics.kicker: English philosopher · Tabula rasa, natural rights, and the social contract
topics.briefing: John Locke believed every baby’s mind starts out as a blank slate, or tabula rasa, filled in only later by experience. In his _Two Treatises of Government_, he argued that all people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that a government which tramples those rights can rightfully be overthrown. Decades later, Thomas Jefferson echoed Locke’s language when he wrote the Declaration of Independence.

sample.note: 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This thinker argued that governments gain their power only from the consent of the people they govern, and that people who agree to form a society give up some freedom from a peaceful “state of nature” in exchange for protection. He wrote that no one ought to harm another “in his life, health, liberty, or possessions.”
tossups.r: That line comes from a work that inspired the Declaration of Independence. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who described the mind at birth as a “blank slate.”

tossups.p: This philosopher wrote that “no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions,” and argued that people may rightfully overthrow a government that fails to protect those rights. He also attacked atheists as untrustworthy citizens in a work defending religious tolerance among Christians.
tossups.r: That work on toleration appeared around the same time as an essay describing the mind as a “blank slate,” or tabula rasa. For 10 points, name this English philosopher whose social contract theory inspired the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: In the first of a pair of treatises, this philosopher set out to “overthrow” the “false principles and foundation” of Sir Robert Filmer, who had defended the divine right of kings. The second treatise then argued that legitimate government rests only on the consent of the governed.
tossups.r: The two are usually published together as his _Two Treatises of Government_. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who believed the mind begins as a blank slate.

tossups.p: This philosopher trained as a physician and once worked as personal doctor and secretary to the Earl of Shaftesbury. He later argued that a government’s power comes only from the consent of the people, not from the divine right of kings claimed by writers like Robert Filmer.
tossups.r: That argument appears in his _Two Treatises of Government_, while a separate essay of his describes minds at birth as blank slates. For 10 points, name this English philosopher, a major influence on the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: German philosopher Gottfried Leibniz wrote a chapter-by-chapter rebuttal to one of this man’s books, defending the idea of innate ideas that this man had rejected. Bishop George Berkeley also criticized this same book, rejecting its split between “primary” and “secondary” qualities.
tossups.r: That book, _An Essay Concerning Human Understanding_, argued the mind begins as a tabula rasa, or blank slate. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who also wrote _Two Treatises of Government_.

tossups.p: This philosopher distinguished “primary qualities,” like shape and size that truly exist in an object, from “secondary qualities,” like color and taste, which he said exist only in a perceiving mind. He proposed that personal identity depends on a continuous chain of memory, not an unchanging soul.
tossups.r: Those ideas appear in his _Essay Concerning Human Understanding_. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who described the mind at birth as a “blank slate.”

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that people are born with no innate ideas at all, gaining every idea only through experience, a claim that made him a founder of empiricism. He was also a member of the Royal Society and a close friend of the scientist Robert Boyle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English philosopher who compared the newborn mind to a tabula rasa, or “blank slate,” in his _Essay Concerning Human Understanding_.

tossups.p: This philosopher’s two-part political work refutes Robert Filmer’s defense of absolute monarchy before laying out a theory of natural rights. He published that work anonymously, fearing political trouble, and its authorship was only confirmed after his death.
tossups.r: That work, _Two Treatises of Government_, named rights to life, liberty, and property. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who also wrote _An Essay Concerning Human Understanding_.

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that a government is bound by a trust: if rulers break that trust by threatening the natural rights of the people, the people regain the right to resist and form a new government. He laid out that theory of social contract in two linked treatises.
tossups.r: He listed life, liberty, and property as the natural rights that government must protect. For 10 points, name this English philosopher, a major influence on Thomas Jefferson.

tossups.p: This philosopher wrote _A Letter Concerning Toleration_ arguing that governments should allow most Christian groups to worship freely, though he still distrusted atheists. He is sometimes called the “Father of Liberalism” for his influence on individual rights and limited government.
tossups.r: He is better remembered for describing the mind at birth as a tabula rasa. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who wrote _Two Treatises of Government_.

tossups.p: This philosopher proposed that objects only truly possess qualities like shape, size, and motion, while qualities like color and smell exist only inside a perceiving mind. He set out this distinction between primary and secondary qualities in an essay about human understanding.
tossups.r: That essay also compares the newborn mind to a blank slate. For 10 points, name this English philosopher whose ideas about natural rights to life, liberty, and property inspired the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: This philosopher imagined a peaceful “state of nature” that people leave behind by consenting to form a government, a very different picture from the violent state of nature described by Thomas Hobbes. He is considered a founder of classical liberalism.
tossups.r: He named life, liberty, and property as rights no government may violate. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who described the newborn mind as a blank slate.

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that complex ideas are built up from simple ideas that enter the mind only through the senses or through reflecting on one’s own thoughts. He rejected the theory, defended by thinkers like Descartes, that some ideas are innate from birth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English empiricist who wrote _An Essay Concerning Human Understanding_ and compared the mind at birth to a tabula rasa.

tossups.p: This philosopher’s _Essay Concerning Human Understanding_ describes the mind at birth as “white paper, void of all characters,” a phrase that became famous as tabula rasa. He also worked for England’s Board of Trade later in life.
tossups.r: His _Two Treatises of Government_ argued that revolution is justified when rulers violate natural rights. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who influenced the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: This philosopher’s Second Treatise argues that property is created when a person mixes their own labor with something found in nature, like land or wood. His First Treatise, meanwhile, directly refutes Sir Robert Filmer’s _Patriarcha_.
tossups.r: Together, those works are usually printed as _Two Treatises of Government_. For 10 points, name this English philosopher who described the newborn mind as a tabula rasa.

trap.title: Which social contract thinker?
trap.body: Locke, Thomas Hobbes, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau all wrote about a “social contract” and a “state of nature,” so hearing those words alone is not enough to know which one to buzz. Each philosopher pictured the state of nature very differently and drew a different conclusion about government from it.
trap.fix: Hobbes: a violent state of nature (“war of every man against every man”), _Leviathan_, an all-powerful ruler. Locke: a peaceful state of nature, natural rights to life, liberty, and property, tabula rasa, limited government by consent. Rousseau: the “general will” and the idea that people are naturally good but corrupted by society.

topics.name: Karl Marx
topics.kicker: German philosopher and economist · Co-wrote The Communist Manifesto
topics.briefing: Karl Marx argued that history is driven by struggle between economic classes, especially between factory owners and the workers they employed. With his collaborator Friedrich Engels, he published _The Communist Manifesto_ in 1848, famously declaring that “a spectre is haunting Europe” and calling on “workers of the world” to unite. His later, longer work, _Das Kapital_, became one of the most influential critiques of capitalism ever written.

tossups.p: This thinker developed the theory of historical materialism, the idea that a society’s economic system shapes its history, politics, and ideas. He coined the term “commodity fetishism” to describe how people see the value of goods as natural instead of the result of human labor.
tossups.r: After this man died, his collaborator finished the final volumes of his massive critique of capitalism. For 10 points, name this German thinker who, with Friedrich Engels, wrote _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: Twentieth-century philosopher Karl Popper criticized this man’s use of “historicism” to predict the future of society in Popper’s book _The Open Society and Its Enemies_. This man’s most famous pamphlet opens by describing “a spectre” that is “haunting Europe.”
tossups.r: That pamphlet, co-written with Friedrich Engels, describes a struggle between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. For 10 points, name this German philosopher who wrote _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: This thinker claimed that history repeats itself, “first as tragedy, then as farce,” while describing the rise of Napoleon’s nephew in _The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Napoleon_. He also described a “spectre” that is “haunting Europe” while discussing a long history of class struggle.
tossups.r: That same pamphlet described conflict between the proletariat and the bourgeois classes. For 10 points, name this German philosopher who wrote _Das Kapital_ and co-wrote _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: In a work subtitled “A Critique of Political Economy,” this thinker introduced the idea of “commodity fetishism.” A different work of his begins with the line, “A spectre is haunting Europe.”
tossups.r: This philosopher described the class struggle between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat and wrote _Das Kapital_. For 10 points, name this thinker who worked with Friedrich Engels on _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: In a critique of Hegel’s _Elements of the Philosophy of Right_, this thinker described religion as “the opium of the people.” He discussed “commodity fetishism” in a work subtitled “Critique of Political Economy.”
tossups.r: This thinker claimed a “spectre is haunting Europe” while writing about class struggle with Friedrich Engels. For 10 points, name this German philosopher, the author of _Das Kapital_, who called on “workers of the world” to “unite.”

tossups.p: This thinker wrote that philosophers had only ever interpreted the world, when the real point was to change it, in his _Theses on Feuerbach_ [“FOY-er-bahk”]. He also called religion the “opium of the people” in a critique of Hegel.
tossups.r: In another work, this thinker claimed all history was a “history of class struggles” and commanded the proletarians of the world to unite. For 10 points, name this collaborator of Friedrich Engels who wrote _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: This thinker used the example of twenty yards of linen traded for gold to compare the commodity-form and money-form of value. He also developed a theory of surplus value, which he said drives capitalist profit.

tossups.p: This thinker wrote that history repeats itself, “first as tragedy, then as farce,” in _The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Napoleon_. He also wrote that “a spectre is haunting Europe” in a pamphlet urging the proletariat to revolt against the bourgeoisie.
tossups.r: That pamphlet was co-written with Friedrich Engels. For 10 points, name this German philosopher who also wrote _Das Kapital_.

tossups.p: This thinker argued that the “exchange value” of a good is determined by the labor needed to produce it, a theory now called the labor theory of value. He also wrote, “From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs,” in his _Critique of the Gotha Programme_.
tossups.r: He claimed that “the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.” For 10 points, name this author of _Das Kapital_ and _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: This thinker’s _Theses on Feuerbach_ criticized earlier philosophy for merely interpreting the world. In a book called _The Poverty of Philosophy_, he also criticized the anarchist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.
tossups.r: This critic of Hegel wrote that “a spectre” was “haunting Europe” and told the proletariat to unite against the bourgeoisie. For 10 points, name this German economist and author of _Das Kapital_, who wrote _The Communist Manifesto_ with Friedrich Engels.

tossups.p: This thinker’s 1841 doctoral dissertation compared the ancient philosophers Democritus and Epicurus. Later, he settled in London after being expelled from several European countries for his radical writings, and he is buried there in Highgate Cemetery.
tossups.r: This philosopher argued that economic systems drive the “class struggle” that shapes history. For 10 points, name this German thinker who wrote _Das Kapital_ and co-wrote _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: This thinker was born in the Prussian city of Trier and trained as a philosopher before turning to economics. Friedrich Engels, his lifelong collaborator, helped support this man and his family financially for years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German thinker whose _Communist Manifesto_ calls for the “workers of the world” to “unite,” and whose _Das Kapital_ critiques capitalism.

tossups.p: This thinker described a long “history of class struggles” between the bourgeoisie, who own factories and land, and the proletariat, who sell their labor. His theory that a society’s economic base shapes its politics and culture is called historical materialism.
tossups.r: This philosopher’s _Das Kapital_ built on these ideas to critique capitalism. For 10 points, name this German thinker who co-wrote _The Communist Manifesto_ with Friedrich Engels.

tossups.p: This thinker’s massive critique of capitalism was left unfinished at his death; Friedrich Engels edited and published its final two volumes using this man’s notes. Its first volume explains how capitalists profit from “surplus value” created by workers’ labor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher and economist, the author of _Das Kapital_ and co-author of _The Communist Manifesto_.

tossups.p: This thinker’s most famous pamphlet predicts that capitalism will eventually collapse under its own contradictions as the proletariat rises up against the bourgeoisie. It ends by urging “working men of all countries” to unite.
tossups.r: That 1848 pamphlet, written with Friedrich Engels, opens by warning that “a spectre is haunting Europe.” For 10 points, name this German philosopher and economist who also wrote _Das Kapital_.

topics.name: Socrates
topics.kicker: Ancient Greek philosopher · Taught by asking tough questions, not lecturing
topics.briefing: Socrates never wrote a single word, yet he’s often called the father of Western philosophy. He spent his days in the markets of Athens asking ordinary people hard questions about justice, courage, and the good life, daring them to defend what they thought they knew. His constant questioning eventually got him arrested, tried, and sentenced to death by poison.

sample.note: the 6 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This philosopher claimed to be guided by a private inner voice, his daimonion, that only ever warned him away from mistakes. In Aristophanes’ comedy _The Clouds_, he is mocked as a fraud who hangs suspended in a basket at his “Think-shop,” teaching students to make a weak argument beat a strong one.
tossups.r: He married a woman named Xanthippe and had three sons. For 10 points, name this Athenian philosopher sentenced to death by drinking hemlock, the teacher of Plato.

tossups.p: In one dialogue, this philosopher leads an enslaved boy through a geometry problem about doubling a square’s area, using it to argue that all learning is really remembering. A second source for his ideas, besides Plato, is the _Memorabilia_, written by his student Xenophon.
tossups.r: He never wrote a word himself. For 10 points, name this Athenian philosopher put to death by drinking hemlock, best known through the dialogues of Plato.

tossups.p: In Plato’s _Euthyphro_, this man questions a religious expert about the nature of holiness without ever reaching a clear answer. After the Oracle at Delphi told his friend Chaerephon that no one in Athens was wiser than him, he set out to test that claim by questioning everyone he met.
tossups.r: A method of teaching through careful cross-examination still carries his name today. For 10 points, identify this Athenian philosopher who was a teacher of Plato.

tossups.p: Put on trial in 399 BCE on charges brought by Meletus and joined by Anytus and Lycon, this man delivered a defense speech recorded in Plato’s _Apology_, where he compared himself to a gadfly stinging a lazy horse to keep it alert.
tossups.r: He supposedly told the jury that “the unexamined life is not worth living.” For 10 points, name this philosopher convicted of corrupting the youth of Athens and sentenced to drink poison hemlock.

tossups.p: Alcibiades compared this man’s appearance to a Silenus statue — ugly on the outside but full of wisdom within — in Plato’s _Symposium_. Reportedly the son of a stonemason named Sophroniscus and a midwife named Phaenarete, this thinker later compared his own teaching style to his mother’s profession.
tossups.r: He claimed that true wisdom begins with admitting, “I know that I know nothing.” For 10 points, name this Athenian philosopher, the teacher of Plato.

tossups.p: This man served Athens as a hoplite soldier in the Peloponnesian War, fighting at Potidaea, Delium, and Amphipolis. Friends said he could stand motionless for an entire day lost in thought, and he claimed an inner sign, his daimonion, warned him whenever he was about to make a mistake.
tossups.r: He wrote nothing himself, so almost everything known about him comes from the dialogues of a devoted student. For 10 points, name this philosopher, the teacher of Plato, who died by drinking hemlock.

tossups.p: In Plato’s _Crito_, this man turns down a wealthy friend’s offer to help him escape from prison, arguing that a citizen owes obedience to the laws of his city even when those laws treat him unjustly. In the _Phaedo_, he spends his final hours calmly discussing whether the soul survives death.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Athenian philosopher who accepted his death sentence and drank poison hemlock rather than flee into exile.

tossups.p: This man compared himself to a midwife who helps other people “give birth” to good ideas rather than ever claiming to have answers of his own. He is remembered mainly through the dialogues of one devoted student, since he himself never published a single written work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Athenian philosopher executed by hemlock, whose most famous student was Plato.

tossups.p: This man’s cross-examining style of teaching — asking question after question until a person’s stated belief collapsed into contradiction — is called the elenchus. Aristophanes mocked this same thinker in the comedy _The Clouds_ as a con artist who hangs suspended in a basket at his own school.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Athenian philosopher sentenced to death for corrupting the youth, a teacher of Plato known for his probing method of questioning.

tossups.p: According to one dialogue, this man guided an enslaved boy through doubling the area of a square without ever directly teaching him, concluding that the boy already “knew” the answer and was simply remembering it. He claimed that the Oracle at Delphi had called him the wisest man in Athens, a claim he spent his life trying to disprove.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this philosopher who turned that search into a habit of public questioning, and who was later sentenced to death by drinking hemlock.

tossups.p: This man’s three sons were reportedly present in his cell on the day of his execution, described in Plato’s _Phaedo_. He was married to a woman named Xanthippe, later remembered — fairly or not — as famously hard to live with.
tossups.r: Facing a jury that convicted him of impiety and corrupting Athens’s youth, he calmly accepted his sentence. For 10 points, name this philosopher who drank poison hemlock rather than beg for mercy or flee the city.

tossups.p: This man once stood in an army camp so lost in thought that, according to one story, he didn’t move for a full day and night. In Plato’s _Symposium_, Alcibiades jokes that this man resembles an ugly little statue of a satyr that opens to reveal golden images inside.
tossups.r: He claimed his own wisdom amounted only to knowing that he knew nothing. For 10 points, name this Athenian philosopher and teacher of Plato, who was sentenced to death by hemlock.

tossups.p: This man asked a religious expert named Euthyphro to define holiness on the steps of a courthouse, but their conversation ends without settling the question. He also questioned politicians, poets, and craftsmen around Athens, concluding that each only thought he knew more than he actually did.
tossups.r: A jury of Athenian citizens found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the young. For 10 points, name this philosopher who accepted a death sentence of drinking hemlock rather than flee Athens.

tossups.p: This philosopher’s father, Sophroniscus, was said to be a stonemason, while his mother, Phaenarete, worked as a midwife — a profession he later compared to his own habit of helping others deliver good ideas. He also fought for Athens as a foot soldier in the Peloponnesian War.
tossups.r: Later tried on charges brought by Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon, he refused his friend Crito’s offer to help him escape prison. For 10 points, name this philosopher who drank hemlock after being convicted of corrupting Athens’s youth.

tossups.p: Rather than lecture, this man preferred to walk through the Athenian marketplace asking ordinary citizens to defend definitions of justice, courage, and piety, often reducing them to confused silence. He believed an inner divine sign warned him away from wrongdoing, though it never told him what to actually do.
tossups.r: He taught Plato, who recorded his conversations since he never wrote anything down himself. For 10 points, name this philosopher who was sentenced to death and drank poison hemlock after being convicted of corrupting the youth of Athens.

trap.title: Socrates, Plato, or Aristotle?
trap.body: These three Greek philosophers form a teaching chain: Socrates taught Plato, and Plato taught Aristotle. A clue mentioning the Lyceum, the four causes, or tutoring Alexander the Great means Aristotle, not Socrates. A clue mentioning the theory of Forms, the _Republic_, or an Academy almost always means Plato.
trap.fix: Socrates is the one who never wrote anything down. If the clue says this person authored or wrote a philosophical treatise, the answer is Plato or Aristotle, not Socrates — Socrates only ever appears as a character inside someone else’s writing.

topics.name: Immanuel Kant
topics.kicker: German Enlightenment philosopher · Ethics of the categorical imperative
topics.briefing: Immanuel Kant spent almost his entire life in one Prussian city, Königsberg, where neighbors supposedly set their clocks by his daily walk. Despite rarely traveling anywhere, he produced some of philosophy’s biggest ideas, including the categorical imperative, a test for figuring out whether an action is truly moral. His _Critique of Pure Reason_ remains one of the most influential, and most difficult, books ever written.

sample.note: 15 real QBReader tossups (3 Middle School/Easy High School + 12 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This thinker argued that judging a steak “good to eat” is a merely “agreeable” reaction, different from recognizing something as truly beautiful. Arthur Schopenhauer later wrote an extended critique of this philosopher’s ideas, particularly his concept of the “thing-in-itself.”
tossups.r: This philosopher argued that acting morally means following a rule you could want everyone else to follow too. For 10 points, name this German philosopher who developed the categorical imperative and wrote _Critique of Pure Reason_.

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that we can only perceive things as existing at the same time if they stand in “thoroughgoing interaction,” a response to Leibniz’s view that separate substances never truly affect one another. He also claimed that mathematical truths, like “7 plus 5 equals 12,” are known before experience yet still add new information, calling them synthetic a priori.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher who argued that reading the empiricist David Hume woke him from his “dogmatic slumber,” and who wrote _Critique of Pure Reason_.

tossups.p: This philosopher distinguished “noumena,” things as they really are, from “phenomena,” things as we experience them, arguing the human mind can only ever know the second kind. He imagined an ideal community called the “Kingdom of Ends,” where every rational being treats others as valuable in themselves rather than as tools.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher whose ethical theory, deontology, centers on an unconditional rule called the categorical imperative.

tossups.p: This philosopher proposed that a world made up entirely of constitutional republics could achieve lasting peace, in an essay titled _Perpetual Peace_. In a different work, he argued that any defense of lying — even to a murderer asking where a friend is hiding — fails to respect other people as rational beings.
tossups.r: His most famous ethical rule asks whether the reasoning behind your action could become a universal law for everyone. For 10 points, name this German philosopher, author of _Critique of Pure Reason_.

tossups.p: This philosopher defined Enlightenment as “man’s emergence from his self-imposed immaturity” and urged his readers to “dare to know” in a short, famous essay. He also compared historical religion to “clothing” layered over a more basic rational religion in _Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German Enlightenment philosopher who proposed the categorical imperative in _Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals_.

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that “humanity itself is dignity,” meaning every rational person deserves respect simply for being rational. He divided one late work, _The Metaphysics of Morals_, into a “Doctrine of Right” covering laws and a “Doctrine of Virtue” covering ethics.
tossups.r: His most famous principle holds that you should act only according to rules you could will to become universal laws. For 10 points, name this German philosopher who wrote _Critique of Pure Reason_.

tossups.p: This philosopher rejected the ontological argument for God’s existence while developing his theory of “synthetic a priori” judgments in his most famous work. He explained that mental structures called schemata connect abstract concepts to the raw material of sensory experience.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher, author of _Critique of Pure Reason_, who formulated the categorical imperative.

tossups.p: This philosopher blended the rationalist and empiricist traditions, trying to answer skeptical challenges David Hume raised about cause and effect. He listed humanity, universal law, and the “Kingdom of Ends” as three different formulations of one single moral principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher who wrote three major Critiques, including one on Pure Reason, and who is remembered for the categorical imperative.

tossups.p: This philosopher spent nearly his entire life in the Prussian city of Königsberg, reportedly so punctual on his daily walk that neighbors set their clocks by him. He argued that the human mind actively shapes space and time rather than passively receiving them, a view called transcendental idealism.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher who wrote _Critique of Pure Reason_ and developed the categorical imperative.

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that lying is always wrong, even to a murderer asking for a friend’s hiding place, a position he defended in an essay responding to Benjamin Constant. He is remembered as a founder of deontological ethics, judging actions by duty and rule rather than by their results.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher whose _Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals_ introduced the categorical imperative.

tossups.p: This philosopher’s idea of the “noumenon” was later reinterpreted by his critic Arthur Schopenhauer in _The World as Will and Representation_. He claimed that rational beings should always be treated as ends in themselves, never merely as a means to someone else’s goal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher who wrote _Critique of Pure Reason_ and proposed the categorical imperative in his ethics.

tossups.p: This philosopher argued that genuine knowledge requires both raw sensory data and the mind’s own built-in structures for organizing it, rejecting purely rationalist and purely empiricist accounts on their own. His moral theory lists universal law, humanity, and the kingdom of ends as three equivalent ways of stating the same basic duty.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German Enlightenment philosopher, the author of _Critique of Pure Reason_ and the formulator of the categorical imperative.

tossups.p: This philosopher wrote that reading the Scottish philosopher David Hume woke him from his “dogmatic slumber” and pushed him toward a new theory of knowledge. His three major works, covering pure reason, practical reason, and judgment, are simply known as his three Critiques.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher remembered for the categorical imperative, an unconditional rule for moral action.

tossups.p: This philosopher claimed that mathematical statements are a strange category of knowledge, known independently of experience yet not just true by definition, calling them synthetic a priori truths. He also argued that history is slowly guiding humanity toward a federation of peaceful constitutional republics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German philosopher, author of _Critique of Pure Reason_, who introduced the categorical imperative in his ethical writings.

tossups.p: This philosopher insisted that acting morally means obeying self-given rational rules rather than chasing good outcomes, a position called deontological ethics. He is remembered for distinguishing things as they appear to us from things as they truly are, calling the two phenomena and noumena.
tossups.r: This philosopher developed an unconditional moral rule, the categorical imperative, in his book _Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals_. For 10 points, name this German Enlightenment philosopher, author of _Critique of Pure Reason_.

topics.name: The Prince
topics.kicker: Machiavelli’s 1513 guide for rulers · How to seize and keep power
topics.briefing: After losing his government job in 1512, a Florentine diplomat named Niccolò Machiavelli wrote a blunt how-to guide for rulers in 1513, hoping to win back a position. Instead of preaching about how rulers should be good, it coolly explained how rulers actually keep power — arguing that a prince should act like both a lion and a fox, and that it is safer to be feared than loved.
